description: The Great Terror of 1936-38: show trials, the NKVD, purges and the gulag system.
content_html:
The Murder of Kirov and the Start of the Terror

On 1 December 1934, Sergei Kirov — the popular Leningrad party boss and a potential rival to Stalin — was shot dead in his office. The assassin was a young Communist named Leonid Nikolayev. Stalin immediately used the murder to justify a sweeping crackdown on “enemies of the state.” Within days, emergency laws were passed allowing executions without proper trial. Whether Stalin ordered the killing himself has never been conclusively proved, but historians widely agree that he exploited it ruthlessly.

The assassination triggered a wave of arrests and executions in Leningrad. More broadly, it began a pattern that would culminate in the Great Terror of 1936–38, a period of political violence unprecedented even by Soviet standards. Historians estimate that approximately 750,000 people were executed during the Terror and at least a million more died in labour camps.

Key Fact

The Great Terror ran from approximately 1936 to 1938. Historians estimate around 750,000 executions took place during this period. It targeted party members, Red Army officers, intellectuals, ethnic minorities and ordinary citizens alike.

The Moscow Show Trials

Between 1936 and 1938 Stalin staged three major show trials that became the public face of the Terror. The defendants — including prominent Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin — confessed to fantastical crimes: plotting to murder Stalin, sabotaging industry, spying for Nazi Germany and Japan. The confessions were extracted through months of psychological pressure, sleep deprivation and threats to defendants' families.

The first trial in August 1936 resulted in the execution of Zinoviev and Kamenev. The second trial in January 1937 saw a further group of party officials executed. The third trial in March 1938 included Nikolai Bukharin, whom Lenin had described in his Testament as “the favourite of the whole Party” and the party’s “most valuable and biggest theoretician.” Bukharin was found guilty and shot. International observers present at the trials were often shocked by the defendants' apparent willingness to confess; only later was the full picture of coercion understood.

The confessions were not freely given. The NKVD (secret police) used prolonged interrogation, physical abuse, sleep deprivation and threats against family members. Some defendants also confessed out of a twisted sense of party loyalty — believing that a public confession, however false, might serve the party's interests. Bukharin's confession at his 1938 trial was particularly complex: he confessed in general terms while subtly denying specific charges, a strategy documented in his private correspondence and later analysed by historians.

The NKVD was headed from 1936 to 1938 by Nikolai Yezhov, whose name gave the Terror its Russian nickname: the Yezhovshchina (Yezhov era). Yezhov was himself arrested in 1938 and executed in 1940 — an ironic victim of the system he had overseen. In Stalinist photographs, he was later erased entirely, replaced by empty background.

The Purge of the Red Army

One of the most strategically damaging aspects of the Terror was the purge of the Red Army. Between 1937 and 1938, Stalin had approximately three of the five Soviet marshals, 13 of 15 army commanders, and a very large proportion of senior officers arrested and shot or imprisoned. The exact figures remain disputed by historians, but the scale of the devastation to military leadership was enormous.

This purge left the Red Army without experienced commanders at precisely the moment when war with Nazi Germany was becoming increasingly likely. When Germany invaded in June 1941, many Soviet military failures in the early weeks were at least partly attributed to the destruction of the officer corps in the Terror.

Key Fact

The purge of the Red Army between 1937–38 removed a large proportion of its senior commanders. This severely weakened Soviet military capability at a critical time, contributing to the disasters of 1941 when Germany invaded.

The Gulag System

Alongside executions, millions of Soviet citizens were sentenced to the gulag — a vast network of forced labour camps spread across the Soviet Union, particularly in Siberia and the Far North. By 1938 the gulag population may have numbered over one and a half million prisoners, though estimates vary. Conditions were brutal: prisoners worked in freezing temperatures mining gold, felling timber or digging canals, with minimal food and clothing.

The gulag became one of the most powerful symbols of Stalinist repression. The writer Alexander Solzhenitsyn, who spent years in the camps, later wrote the most famous accounts of gulag life. His One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, published in 1962 during the brief Khrushchev Thaw, was the first Soviet-published account to describe camp conditions openly.

The Terror was not confined to party elites. Mass operations targeted ethnic minorities (particularly Poles, Germans and Koreans living inside the USSR), factory managers, engineers, academics and ordinary workers denounced by neighbours or colleagues. The culture of denunciation spread fear throughout Soviet society — people were afraid to write letters, speak freely or associate with those who had been arrested.

Fear was, in part, the point. A terrorised population was easier to control. At the same time, the Terror destroyed exactly the kinds of skilled, experienced and independently minded people that the Soviet economy and military most needed. Historians debate how far this was a calculated strategy by Stalin or a system that grew beyond any individual's control.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain a Consequence’ questions on the Terror, make sure you identify what changed and explain why that change was significant. For example: the purge of the Red Army weakened Soviet military capacity, which meant the USSR was badly exposed when Germany invaded in 1941 — this was a consequence that stretched beyond the Terror itself. For ‘Evaluate an Interpretation’ questions, remember you must both agree and disagree using specific knowledge before reaching your own substantiated judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Terror (1936–38) began after the murder of Kirov in 1934 and included show trials in which Old Bolsheviks like Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed to fabricated crimes and were executed.
  • The NKVD under Yezhov carried out mass arrests, executions and deportations to the gulag. The purge of the Red Army severely weakened Soviet military capacity before the Second World War.
  • The gulag was a vast network of forced labour camps. Writers such as Alexander Solzhenitsyn later exposed conditions there to the world.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Moscow show trials of 1936–1938.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: defendants confessed to fabricated crimes such as plotting against Stalin or sabotaging industry; confessions were extracted through coercion by the NKVD; prominent Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin were tried and executed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the gulag system under Stalin.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: a vast network of forced labour camps across Siberia and the Far North; prisoners carried out dangerous work such as mining and logging in extreme cold; the gulag population numbered over a million by the late 1930s; conditions were deliberately harsh with minimal food and clothing.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed, or one developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the purge of the Red Army between 1937 and 1938.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a consequence and explain why it followed from the purge. Strong answers trace causal chains. Top response: the purge removed the most experienced senior commanders, leaving the Red Army without effective leadership; when Germany invaded in June 1941, the USSR suffered catastrophic early defeats that might have been avoided with a more experienced officer corps.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise consequence identified, causal chain explained, supported with specific knowledge.
Secure: consequence identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: consequence identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the murder of Kirov in 1934 for the development of Stalinist terror.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: Stalin immediately passed emergency laws allowing executions without full trial and used the assassination to justify mass arrests in Leningrad. Over time: the Kirov murder was the trigger for the Great Terror of 1936–38, which killed hundreds of thousands and fundamentally reshaped Soviet political culture through fear.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways or at two time points, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point, partial knowledge.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of the Great Terror:

“The Great Terror was caused primarily by Stalin’s personal paranoia rather than any genuine threat to his regime.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree, then reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: the confessions were fabricated; the accused including Bukharin had shown loyalty to the party; the show trials targeted people who posed no realistic threat; Yezhov himself was purged in 1938 suggesting the terror had a self-perpetuating logic fed by Stalin's suspicion.

Disagreement: the USSR faced genuine external threats from Nazi Germany and Japan; there was a history of internal factional opposition from Left and Right; fear of a 'fifth column' had some historical basis in the Civil War era; some historians argue Stalin had rational political goals including eliminating potential rivals and creating a compliant population.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence for both sides, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was the use of terror the most important way in which Stalin maintained control of the Soviet Union? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For the argument: the show trials eliminated potential rivals; mass arrests created a culture of fear that prevented organised opposition; the NKVD surveilled the entire population; the gulag removed dissidents from society.

Alternative methods: propaganda and the Cult of Stalin built genuine loyalty; economic successes of the Five Year Plans gave Stalin legitimacy; censorship controlled information; the party structure rewarded loyalty.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple methods, clear judgement with supporting evidence.
Secure: two or more methods explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: methods listed or described, limited weighing.
Emerging: one method or descriptive throughout.

glossary_terms.definition: The period of mass political repression in the Soviet Union from approximately 1936 to 1938, characterised by show trials, mass arrests and executions.
Politically staged public trials in which the accused confessed to fabricated crimes, designed to eliminate political rivals and intimidate the population.
The Soviet secret police under Stalin, responsible for mass arrests, interrogations, executions and running the gulag labour camps.
A network of Soviet forced labour camps where political prisoners and convicted criminals were held in brutal conditions, often in remote regions.
Soviet author who survived the gulag and later exposed its horrors in works such as One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962) and The Gulag Archipelago.
Nikolai Yezhov, head of the NKVD from 1936 to 1938, who oversaw the Great Terror and was himself arrested and executed in 1940.
